content.thinking:
I'm planning the composition carefully before writing any code: a red panda perched on a mossy stone in Genshin style, working out proportions for the rock and the panda's body, tail, and stance so the scene reads believably at scale.

Now I'm shaping the stone using a lathe profile with a flattened top and painting it with a procedural moss/rock pattern -- blending noise-based mottling so the top surface reads as mossy while the sides stay stony.

I'm also scaling down the overall composition for believable proportions, setting stone top height around 0.42-0.56m, then building the panda's skeleton: feet sunk slightly into the moss, hips and chest positioned to create a stocky arched spine typical of a red panda, working out the chain of points for the body curve.

Defining spine joints...

Instead of separate sweeps, I think it's simpler to loft the body as one continuous catmull path combining the spine and neck points, then build the head as a separate part attached at the head joint.

Then I add the neck chain spanning two joints up to the head, with the head positioned forward and slightly down to match a red panda's typical low, forward-held posture, sized proportionally smaller than the body.

For the head itself, I'm using a scaled sphere centered forward on the head joint, building a red panda face with rusty-red fur on top, white cheeks and muzzle, dark tear marks under the eyes, a black nose, and ears that are red outside with white inner tufts. Now I'm setting up the anime-style eyes with decals.

Choosing a teal-green iris color that'll look charming against the red fur, positioning the eye decals on the skull surface with appropriate azimuth and elevation offsets for size and placement. Then I'm adding the white cream snout sphere, a small dark nose tip, and a separate lower jaw piece scaled and positioned beneath the muzzle.

I'm setting up the jaw joint to hinge forward from the head, then adding a dark reddish-brown tear-mark decal running from the eye down to the muzzle using a tapered SVG stripe shape, plus considering a patch of white cheek fur.

For the cheek fur, I'm scattering card-based tufts across the skull surface, filtering hits by position so they cluster near the cheeks, and rendering each with a pointed white fur-tuft texture sized and angled to lie against the head.

Now I'm building the ears as extruded rounded-triangle outlines positioned near the top of the head, giving them thickness and orienting them to face forward.

I'm realizing the mirrored side's thickness direction flips the normal backward, so I need to figure out the right axis combination so both ears face +Z regardless of the sign flip -- possibly by adjusting the outline orientation itself rather than the extrusion vectors.

Working out the ear axes and symmetric outline points...

Placing inner ear detail and considering eyebrow spots and whiskers for red panda realism. Now thinking through the body shape — stocky spine radius tapering from tail to chest — and the coloring scheme, with rusty-orange topside and dark brown/black belly and legs matching real red panda markings.

Working out the tail's ringed pattern with alternating light and dark bands, wrapping the coloring with cel-shading so the rings still read correctly under the lighting model.

Picking the color palette now: bright clean red for the body, warm cream-orange highlights, and a darker shade for the belly to give that Genshin-style contrast.

I'm thinking about adding small fur tufts along the back and a cute accessory - maybe a teal ribbon scarf with a golden bell and tassel, plus a subtle glowing elemental motif to tie into the character theme.

I'm adding floating dendro wisps: tiny glowing green motes and leaf cards near the tail, attached to root bones so they move naturally, along with a gold ring band around the tail base holding a small leaf charm. I'm also scattering moss tufts on the stone base for texture.

Now I'm covering the stone with small glow-capped mushrooms, flowers, and ferns, plus cracks in the rock, and considering projecting a glowing green rune decal onto the stone's front surface to tie in the dendro theme. I'm figuring out placement coordinates so the decal sits just on the faceted stone surface without clipping through it.

For the stone shape itself, I'm building it from a main lathe body plus several flattened boulder satellites and a flat top slab, then wrapping the base with grass cards and moss patches for texture.

On top I'm adding a squashed moss cushion made from a scaled-down sphere, positioned so the panda's feet sink slightly into it. For the stone's lathe profile, I'm defining the radius-height points to get a rounded boulder silhouette with creased edges where corners are sharp.

I'm checking that the profile closes cleanly on the axis without crossing itself, and deciding to skip smoothing to avoid shifting points to negative x — enough points in the profile should give a good shape without it.

Now I'm checking the moss cap's size against the panda's feet positions to make sure the cap covers them properly.

Working out the leg joint positions and bend directions for front and hind legs, checking that limb segment lengths stay within reach of the foot targets while keeping knees/hocks bent plausibly forward or back.

I'll use "R" for right-side naming, with "leg" roles for hind limbs and "arm" for fore. For the legs I want tapered radii and dark cel-shaded paws, scaled spheres positioned slightly forward with small toe bumps and claw spikes attached to the tip joint of each chain, handling the possible null case.

For the pose, I'm leaning toward keeping a neutral symmetric stance rather than a lifted-paw balancing pose, but giving the tail a dramatic S-curve rising up and back from the hips to suggest a sense of balance.

Reconsidering the tail geometry, I think my first curve was too long relative to the body, so I'm shortening the control points to about 0.6m total length, tapering the radius from thin near the hips to thick and bushy in the middle, then narrowing at the tip, with ring-based cel coloring that darkens near the very end. I'm also considering adding fur card tufts along the tail for a fluffier look, though tinting them consistently with the ringed paint pattern is tricky since the paint is only sampled at the root.

For the body, I'm defining the fur edge shading using the main red tone against a dark chestnut belly color, skipping ink outlines to match a Genshin-style soft look, and adding a mottled orange saddle pattern layered under the cel shading for subtle color variation.

For the head, I'm working out a position-based paint function that determines cream versus red-brown regions using zigzag boundary thresholds relative to the skull center, trying to approximate the red panda's characteristic white cheek and muzzle patches against the reddish forehead and streak.

Now I'm figuring out the nose, lips, and under-chin details, then moving to the scarf accessory — planning to build it as a closed-loop sweep ring around the neck using the frame at a specific point along the neck chain, with catmull-rom interpolation to smooth the band.

For the hanging scarf tail, I'm positioning a flat extruded banner shape at the front of the neck, dropping down along the chest, working out the outline points and coordinates so it drapes naturally in front of the body without floating away from the chest surface.

Confirming the thickness vector math checks out. Now I'm planning the decorative details: a gold trim strip and tassel spheres at the scarf tail end, a small golden bell at the knot, and dendro-themed glowing green orbs floating near the tail and head with halo rings, assigned to the tail joint bone. I'm also considering adding a golden bracelet.

Adding gold anklet rings around each of the four legs using a sweep at a specific point along the leg chain, sizing the ring and sweep radius to match the leg's taper. I'm also planning fur tufts along the spine ridge, tail, and ears using card textures, writing an SVG tuft shape for fur cards and thinking through a separate green moss tuft texture variant.

Now I'm designing grass blade SVGs in varied greens, plus a small flower shape and mushroom meshes built from cylinder stems and half-sphere caps -- mixing warm cream-and-coral mushrooms with glowing teal dendro-style ones, using position-based paint to add spots on the caps. I'm also working out how to drape hanging moss along the stone's edge using a ring of frames with leaning card geometry to create a drip effect.

I'm now figuring out the correct card orientation so the moss drips hang edge-on versus face-on depending on position, and designing the moss drip SVG texture to taper from a wide attached base to a narrow tip so it reads correctly when hanging upside-down from the cap's equator.

Checking the math, I realize the cap's cards would actually sit hidden inside the stone's radius at those heights, so I'm adjusting the stone's profile and the cap size to avoid the overlap. Instead of fixing the cap geometry precisely, I decide it's simpler to scatter moss clumps directly onto the stone's surface, filtering hits to the upper region and treating them as small standing grass-blade cards.

I'll blend in moss coverage based on surface normal and height so the upper, more exposed parts of the stone get more growth, which should give enough visual volume without fussing over exact overlap math. I'll also add a glowing rune decal on the stone, scatter a few flattened pebbles and flower cards around the base on the floor, and ring the stone with upward-facing grass cards at a radius that keeps the whole prop around a meter wide.

Now I'm setting up imports for the build script, pulling in the geometry builder, frame helper, noise/paint utilities, IK limb solver, SVG texture tools, and toon shading kit, making sure every import actually gets used since unused ones will error. I'm defining the color palette for the creature, starting with reds, rust tones, and belly/cream shades before laying out the metadata export.

I'm building the shaded coat, leg, paw, and nose colors using the cel toon-shading helper, then working through the tail's paint logic -- trying to figure out whether to use a card-based ring pattern or compute distance along the tail's path to drive the color transitions, while weighing the performance cost of sampling the path per texel.

I'll scatter cards along the tail sweep, grouping hits by band and coloring them with flow directions derived from the tail path's tangent at each closest point. Then I'm building the spine chain from hip to neck using catmull curves, defining joint names and parent relationships for each segment.

Working out neck and head placement, making sure the head joint sits forward of the neck with the skull proportioned for a chibi panda look, keeping overall body length reasonable relative to the tail root and nose position. Now I'm setting up the body sweep along the spine.

Defining radius functions...

Now setting up the leg loop, building front limb chains symmetrically for left and right sides with shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints attached to the spine.

Setting hind leg roots and targets now, bending the knee forward with toes pointing forward for the hind feet.

For the hind limb I'm trying a 3-segment setup with hip, knee, hock, and foot joints, checking the segment lengths against the distance to make sure the chain reaches properly, then adding paw spheres at the wrist joints.

Positioning the toe beans and tiny cream claw spikes...

Now I'm sketching the head helper function for local offsets, and starting to define the skull part with its own geometry and placement.

Writing face paint logic...

Still writing head coloring logic...

Now I'm placing eye decals, finding symmetric hit points around the skull surface and attaching mirrored eye textures with iris color at each location.

Setting the tear stripe to mirror symmetrically from the eye corner toward the mouth in dark red, then placing the nose as a small dark sphere on the muzzle.

Now I'm working out the muzzle, jaw, tongue, tiny fangs, and smile-line details so the face reads correctly without the nose poking too far forward, then moving on to building the ears.

The ears get extruded shapes attached to the head bone, tilted outward with a dark red outer layer and a smaller cream inner-fringe shape layered slightly forward to create the classic red panda two-tone ear look. Still working through the exact offsets so the inner fringe sits properly within the outer ear without clipping through it.

Now I'm positioning the cream brow spots above each eye, working out the spherical coordinates on the skull surface by converting the eye's angular position into local head-space x/y/z so the spot lands just above the eye socket with correct curvature.

Next I'm adding thin whisker rods sweeping outward from the muzzle on each side, then setting up cheek fur cards scattered across the skull surface using a filter that restricts them to the lower cheek region, giving each card a lean and bend to simulate tuft flow. I'm skipping extra forehead and ear fur details, then starting on a neck scarf built as a closed catmull-rom sweep around a ring of points positioned along the neck chain.

Writing scarf geometry...

Now I'm figuring out the knot and dangling tail of the scarf, positioning a teal sphere knot against the front of the neck surface and planning a gold bell accent plus a hanging tail that drapes down toward the chest, checking the coordinates line up with the neck's radius and the chest's z-position.

For attaching pieces to the skeleton, I'm deciding to bind the scarf ring to the neck bone for rigidity at rest pose rather than specifying a particular joint. Then I'm adding small glowing motes near the head and tail using tiny icosahedron geometries for a subtle magical floating effect.

I'm also planning glowing leaf cards scattered near the tail, using leaf-shaped textures with colored veins, framed and tilted to float naturally and bound to a specific tail joint. Finally I'm working out mushroom placements on the mossy cap surface near the panda's legs, calculating the curved surface height at each coordinate so the stems sit flush and positioning a small cluster of two or three mushrooms with varying cap sizes.

For binding static props like the stone and mushroom cluster, I'm realizing they should all attach to the root hips joint rather than being auto-assigned to the nearest joint, so I'm setting up an explicit bone reference constant to apply consistently across all the static geometry.

I'm scattering grass cards around the base at random angles and radii with varied sizes, plus adding a handful of small upright flower cards near the floor for extra detail.

For the flowers I'm drawing a simple svg with a green stem and a circular bloom, scaled so the stroke width stays proportional at the target size. For the stone, I'm scattering moss tufts using a surface-based hit scan filtered to upward-facing areas, then adding dark crack-line decals across the surface for texture.

Working out where to place rune and crack decals on the stone requires computing proper hit positions and surface normals using azimuth/elevation offsets from a center point, since projecting directly at a point can miss the surface -- so I'm using surface hit detection around the stone to get accurate placement, with guards for null hits.

Now I'm designing the rune's SVG glyph as a glowing green ring with an inner leaf symbol and tick marks on a transparent background, then moving to body details like flat pebble spheres, scattered back fur tufts with directional lean and flow, and finally working out the tail's alternating color bands to mimic a red panda's ringed pattern using a modulo-based threshold function tied to position along the tail's length.

I'm now placing gold accent rings along the tail and legs, computing their radii by interpolating the tapering body profile at specific points so the metal bands sit flush against the surface without floating or clipping through it.

For the final assembly, I'm verifying all imported helpers like noise, rng, mottle, zigzag, and INK are actually used, then defining the stone and moss surface paints -- blending rock and moss textures based on surface normal and position, wrapped in a cel shader for the toon look.

Now I'm designing the mushroom shapes: a cylindrical stem with a hemispherical cap, using spotted paint textures for color variation, with special glowing variants for bioluminescent mushrooms since paints can't glow so I'll keep those flat-colored. I'm structuring a reusable mushroom-building function that accepts either a plain color or paint for the cap, plus a lit flag for the glowing variety, before moving on to sketching a leaf card texture as an SVG.

Still placing hovering glow-leaf cards and gold-green orbs around the creature, then setting up the stone base lathe sunk slightly into the ground with irregular boulder spheres scattered around it for a natural look.

I'm adding scattered pebbles on the floor and double-checking the paint and shading system for the panda's face, reds, and skin, making sure colors resolve correctly through the cel/mottle paint functions and that part geometry types line up with the expected Fill types.

Still writing limb and tail chain logic...

Adding toe and claw geometry...

Now I'm scattering grass frames around the floor in a ring, building grass and flower textures, placing moss tufts on stone surfaces, and generating scattered tail tuft card groups from surface hits.

Grouping tail tufts by color band, orienting each tuft's lean using the tail path's tangent so they angle outward toward the tip, then finishing up the glow imports and writing the final file with its metadata description.
